terms.gloss: elections; the Roman assemblies that elected the magistrates
evidence: Plin. Ep. 3.20.2: comitiōrum diē, on election day
terms.comment: The Roman people elected its magistrates in the comitia, named after the office at stake (comitia cōnsulāria, praetōria, tribūnicia); to hold an election is comitia habēre (Lewis & Short). Traupman and Morgan–Owens use the word for modern elections. A day on which the assembly could meet was a diēs comitiālis, Morgan–Owens’s election day (M-O; Liv. 25.2.4: prīmō comitiālī diē).
The usual verb for choosing magistrates, of the voters and of the officer who presided (Lewis & Short): cōnsulēs creāre. Traupman gives coöptāre for the choice of Roman senators.

terms.gloss: an election (of a pope or an emperor)
terms.comment: Classically a choice or selection (Cicero, Quintilian); the sense “election” is the Church’s and the Empire’s, as in Morgan–Owens’s seventeenth-century source.
The great enclosure on the Campus Martius where the Roman people voted (Lewis & Short); Traupman uses it for the polls, and saeptum for a polling booth.

terms.gloss: co-opt, elect into a body by its own members
terms.comment: Of senators, priests and colleges choosing new members themselves (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: Proximīs comitiīs in quibusdam tabellīs multa joculāria atque etiam foeda dictū, in ūnā vērō prō candidātōrum nōminibus suffrāgātōrum nōmina inventa sunt.
phrases.english: At the last election some ballots were found to have plenty of jokes on them, and even obscenities, and one had the names of the voters instead of the candidates.
on election day they all asked for ballots
to suffer an upset at the polls
